newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen retreats at US close on Hashimoto comment.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen retreats at US close on Hashimoto comment.

text.p: The dollar fell against the yen on Monday after a remark from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto tying exchange rate stability to Japan's holdings of U.S. Treasury bills sent stocks tumbling.

The Dow Jones industrials unofficially finished 192 points lower at 7,604 after Hashimoto said: "I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange (rate) stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold."
Hashimoto was answering questions after delivering a speech to investors at Columbia University in New York.
It was the second-largest single-day point drop in Dow history, trailing only the 508-point Black Monday market crash of October 19, 1987.
U.S. Treasuries were also weighed down by Hashimoto's remark while gold received a boost higher.
Hashimoto spoke in Japanese and news reports based on English-language translations of his comments caused some market turmoil.
He also noted that in the past, Japan and other countries kept their holdings of U.S. government bonds even though the dollar had fallen.
"So please cooperate with us to stabilize exchange rates in order to prevent us from being tempted to sell U.S. Treasuries and buy gold," Hashimoto said.

The slide in U.S. asset markets dragged the dollar down to close at 114.71/76 yen, well below its 115.30/40 open and its overseas high of 115.67 yen hit after a weekend summit of industrialized nations played down U.S.-Japan trade concerns.
Despite the flurry of dollar trading in late U.S. dealings, a sharp rally in the British pound dominated most of the session's activity, traders said.
The pound continued a rally started on Friday and shot up to its highest level since January 16 versus the dollar and its peak since July 1992 against the mark.

"Sterling's benefitted from a combination of events ranging from a safe haven from European Economic and Monetary Union to the outlook for higher rates," said Bob Near, vice president and trader at the Bank of New York.
Recent UK economic data suggest the Bank of England may raise official interest rates again this cycle to keep inflation in check. The rate hike could come as early as July, dealers said.

Announced last week, UK retail sales surged 1.1 percent in May, with the quarterly rate of increase its highest since July 1988. A separate report showed M4 money supply growth unexpectedly rose in May.
"It looks like the pressure is on the Bank of England to raise rates," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at JP Morgan.

The dollar slipped to 1.7170/80 marks at the close from 1.7210/20 at the open and to 1.4300/10 Swiss francs from 1.4322/32. Meanwhile, sterling jumped to $1.6712/22 from $1.6625/35. Sterling's high was $1.6725 and 2.8738 marks.
A weekend summit between the leaders of the Group of Seven -- the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, and Italy -- yielded no surprises for the currency market.
The dollar benefitted as market fears of a war of words over Japan's growing trade surplus proved unwarranted.
Also, dealers were relieved the G7 leaders did not mention specific currency levels or concerns over dollar strength.
"There were no major signs of tension; no mention at all about currency levels and no indication at all that there were concerns about dollar strength," Leven said.
"If anything, the comments seemed to point to stability at these levels," he added.
At the Denver summit, President Bill Clinton warned Japan that an explosive deterioration in the U.S.-Japan balance of trade could endanger the relationship between the two economic powerhouses.
But Clinton had warned Japan of the risks of its growing trade surplus. Hashimoto blamed the rising surplus to temporary factors and said he did not expect it to continue to climb significantly.

Japan reported last week that its trade surplus tripled in May from a year earlier. U.S. officials are worried that the rise is the start of a steady climb in the surplus back to levels that in the past have led to trade friction.
In other trading, the dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3885/90 from C$1.3893/98. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7518/23 from $0.7503/08.
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
